steps.title: White grapes
steps.body: Alvarinho, the same as Spain's Albariño, gives the fullest, most aromatic wines, especially in Monção e Melgaço. Loureiro gives floral, laurel-scented, citrus wines, mainly in Lima. Arinto, called Pedernã here, gives crisp, lemony acidity. Avesso, in Baião, gives fuller, nuttier wines. Trajadura adds body and softness.

steps.title: Reds and styles
steps.body: Red Vinho Verde, mainly from Vinhão, is deeply coloured, tart and tannic, traditionally served chilled in white bowls with grilled sardines; it's popular locally but rare abroad. Most white Vinho Verde is light, about 9 to 11.5% alcohol, crisp, often with a slight spritz from added carbon dioxide. Single-grape and single-estate wines are more serious.

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its character.
steps.explanation: Vinho Verde's grapes each bring something different.

steps.body: A traditional Vinho Verde's slight spritz once came from malolactic fermentation in bottle; today most producers add carbon dioxide.

steps.prompt: What is Alvarinho called in Spain?
steps.explanation: The same grape across the Minho river.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Alvarinho, Loureiro, Arinto and Avesso are the key whites
Most Vinho Verde is light and slightly spritzy
Red Vinhão is a local, tart, dark speciality
